UNIT 4.1 TRANSACTION ANALYSIS & SCOTS

Analyzing Business Transactions & Significant Classes of Transactions (SCOTs)

Executive Summary & Architectural Context
Accounting is the language of business, but it does not record every organizational event. Building directly on the foundational principles established in Unit 1, the accounting information system captures only financial transactions—events that measurably alter the economic resources (Assets) or obligations (Liabilities) of the business in terms of money. Step 1 of the 10-step accounting cycle transforms commercial activity into quantitative accounting records through Significant Classes of Transactions (SCOTs): Revenue-to-Receipt (R2R), Purchase-to-Payable (P2P), Inventory Management, Fixed Asset (CapEx) Management, and Financial Reporting & Closing. Every transaction is proven by authentic source documents and analyzed using the Architectural Visual Balance Model (Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity).

4.1.1 What is a Business Transaction? (Connecting Back to Unit 1)

In Unit 1 (Introduction to Accounting), we defined accounting via the AICPA standard as "the art of recording, classifying, and summarizing in a significant manner and in terms of money, transactions and events which are, in part at least, of a financial character, and interpreting the results thereof."

Not every business occurrence constitutes an accounting transaction. A business transaction is an economic event between the business entity and an external counterparty (or an internal event such as consumption of supplies or depreciation) that satisfies two strict criteria:

  1. Economic Impact: It causes an immediate, verifiable change in at least two elements of the financial position (Assets, Liabilities, or Owner's Equity).
  2. Reliable Monetary Measurement: It can be quantified objectively in terms of the functional currency (Philippine Pesos, ₱), fulfilling the Monetary Unit Assumption (Unit 2).
Financial Transactions (RECORDABLE)
  • Purchasing merchandise on account with an agreed Sales Invoice (₱85,000).
  • Paying monthly shop rent and receiving an Official Receipt (₱35,000).
  • Signing an enforceable promissory note and receiving cash bank proceeds (₱200,000).
  • Consuming ₱4,000 worth of office supplies during the monthly billing cycle.
  • Billed clients for professional accounting consultations rendered (₱50,000).
Non-Financial Events (NON-RECORDABLE)
  • Hiring a top-tier certified public accountant as new Chief Financial Officer.
  • Signing an exploratory, non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MOU).
  • Sending a price quotation or placing a purchase order before vendor fulfillment.
  • A general economic downturn or customer satisfaction rating fluctuation.
  • Receiving a supplier's catalog with newly revised list prices.
Why Accounting Records Exclusively Capture Quantifiable Financial Data

The General Ledger is not a corporate diary. Under the Monetary Unit Assumption and the Qualitative Characteristic of Verifiability (PFRS Conceptual Framework), accounting systems require an objective, common measuring denominator. While management talent, brand prestige, and employee morale are vital corporate assets, they cannot be reliably assigned a precise peso figure without introducing rampant subjectivity. Therefore, accounting records strictly capture quantifiable financial transactions supported by verifiable source documentation.

4.1.2 The 10 Steps of the Master Accounting Cycle (Visual Roadmap)

The accounting cycle is a systematic, sequential workflow executed every financial period. It transitions from raw daily transactions to audited, finalized financial reports:

Phase 1: Daily Routine Operations (Ongoing Throughout Month / Period)
Step 01 • Identifying
Analyzing Transactions
Examine authentic source documents (invoices, receipts, notes) to determine economic impact on Assets, Liabilities, and Equity.
Step 02 • Recording
Journalizing Entries
Record transactions chronologically in the General Journal (Book of Original Entry) with formal debit and credit accounts.
Step 03 • Classifying
Posting to Ledger
Transfer debits and credits from the General Journal to individual accounts in the General Ledger (Book of Final Entry).
Phase 2: Period-End Summarizing & Diagnostic Testing
Step 04 • Testing
Unadjusted Trial Balance
Extract ending ledger balances to prove mathematical debit/credit equilibrium (Total Debits = Total Credits) prior to adjustments.
Step 05 • Organizing
10-Column Worksheet
Prepare an optional internal spreadsheet organizing unadjusted balances, adjustments, adjusted balances, P&L, and Balance Sheet.
Phase 3: Period-End Accruals & Formal Financial Reporting
Step 06 • Accruals
Adjusting Entries
Journalize and post accruals, deferrals, depreciation, and bad debts under the Accrual Basis of Accounting (PAS 1).
Step 07 • Reporting
Financial Statements
Prepare formal IFRS financial statements: Statement of Profit or Loss, Changes in Equity, Financial Position, and Cash Flows.
Phase 4: Period-End Closing & Resetting for Next Fiscal Year
Step 08 • Zeroing
Closing Entries
Close all temporary/nominal accounts (Revenues, Expenses, Drawings) to Income Summary and transfer net balance to Capital.
Step 09 • Final Verification
Post-Closing Trial Balance
Verify that only real/permanent accounts (Assets, Liabilities, Capital) remain open with debit/credit equality.
Step 10 • Administrative
Reversing Entries
Optional first-day entries of next fiscal period reversing specific accrued expenses and accrued revenues.

4.1.4 The Architectural Visual Balance Model for Debit & Credit

In professional accountancy, the rules of Debit and Credit are not arbitrary memory mnemonics. They derive logically and mathematically from the architectural layout of the Fundamental Accounting Equation and the Statement of Financial Position (Balance Sheet).

THE MASTER ARCHITECTURAL EQUILIBRIUM
ASSETS
LEFT SIDE = DEBIT NORMAL (Dr.)
Increases (+) are recorded as DEBITS.
Decreases (-) are recorded as CREDITS.
=
LIABILITIES + OWNER'S EQUITY
RIGHT SIDE = CREDIT NORMAL (Cr.)
Increases (+) are recorded as CREDITS.
Decreases (-) are recorded as DEBITS.
How Revenues, Expenses, and Drawings Derive Their Debit/Credit Rules from Owner's Equity:

Because Owner's Equity sits on the Right (Credit) side of the equation, any item that directly expands or shrinks Equity inherits its operational debit/credit behavior:

REVENUES (INCOME) CREDIT NORMAL (+)
Revenues represent gross economic inflows that INCREASE Owner's Equity. Because Owner's Equity increases on the Credit side, Revenues naturally increase on the CREDIT side (+ Cr, - Dr).
EXPENSES DEBIT NORMAL (+)
Expenses represent costs incurred that DECREASE Owner's Equity. As a contra-equity element, to reduce a Credit-normal account (Equity), you must record a DEBIT (+ Dr, - Cr).
OWNER'S DRAWINGS DEBIT NORMAL (+)
Owner withdrawals for personal use directly DECREASE Owner's Equity without being an operational expense. As a contra-equity account, Drawings naturally takes a DEBIT balance (+ Dr, - Cr).

Master 9-Quadrant Transaction Analysis Table

Economic Event / Action Element Effect Debit (Dr.) Action Credit (Cr.) Action Balance Model Rationale
Owner invests cash into business Asset ↑, Equity ↑ Debit: Cash Credit: Owner, Capital Left side increases (Dr); Right side increases (Cr).
Borrow cash from bank signing note Asset ↑, Liability ↑ Debit: Cash Credit: Notes Payable Left side increases (Dr); Right side increases (Cr).
Purchase equipment for cash Asset ↑, Asset ↓ Debit: Equipment Credit: Cash Left side reshuffle: one Asset rises (Dr), another falls (Cr).
Purchase supplies on credit Asset ↑, Liability ↑ Debit: Supplies Credit: Accounts Payable Left side increases (Dr); Right side increases (Cr).
Render service for cash Asset ↑, Revenue (Equity) ↑ Debit: Cash Credit: Service Revenue Left side increases (Dr); Equity increases via Revenue (Cr).
Render service on account Asset ↑, Revenue (Equity) ↑ Debit: Accounts Receivable Credit: Service Revenue Left side increases (Dr); Equity increases via Revenue (Cr).
Pay monthly staff salaries Asset ↓, Expense (Equity) ↓ Debit: Salaries Expense Credit: Cash Expense reduces Equity (Dr); Cash reduces Asset (Cr).
Pay supplier on account Asset ↓, Liability ↓ Debit: Accounts Payable Credit: Cash Liability decreases (Dr); Asset decreases (Cr).
Owner withdraws cash for personal use Asset ↓, Drawings (Equity) ↓ Debit: Owner, Personal Credit: Cash Contra-equity rises (Dr); Cash Asset decreases (Cr).
💡 Formative Drill 4.1: Transaction Analysis & SCOTs Micro Check

A business entity receives an unsolicited price quotation and product catalog from an office equipment supplier. Three days later, the purchasing manager places a purchase order (PO) for ₱50,000 of computers. What is the correct accounting treatment upon placing the PO?

Correct! In the P2P cycle, a Purchase Order is an authorization to purchase, not an executed transaction. Accounting records capture only financial transactions where an actual exchange or title transfer occurs (which happens upon receipt of goods supported by a Receiving Report and Sales Invoice).
UNIT 4.2 STEP 2 OF ACCOUNTING CYCLE

Journalizing Business Transactions in the General Journal

Executive Summary & Pedagogical Context
Step 2 of the accounting cycle is Journalizing—recording authenticated commercial transactions in chronological order in the General Journal, legally recognized as the Book of Original Entry. In this module, we examine the complete operational cycle of Archer Stickers Hub, a student-owned retail stall operated by Chris Dela Cruz at De La Salle University (Taft Campus). Students analyze transactions from a big-picture architectural perspective: verifying authentic source documents, assessing the macro impact on the Fundamental Accounting Equation (Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity), translating economic flows into Debit and Credit rules, and executing formal journal entries with strict adherence to professional standards, including the Sacred Blank P/R Rule.

4.2.1 The Big-Picture Information Architecture: From Real-World Events to Legal Journal

In modern commerce, transactions do not spontaneously appear in financial statements. An accountant cannot simply open the General Ledger and write numbers into account balances. Direct-to-ledger posting destroys the narrative context of the transaction, makes compound entries impossible to reconstruct, and creates severe internal control vulnerabilities. Every business event must follow a rigorous 5-Stage Cognitive Pipeline:

Stage 1: Source Document Verification

Every entry must be anchored in objective documentary evidence (e.g., BDO Deposit Slip #DS-001, Commercial Sales Invoice #MVS-1045, Cash Register Tape #001).

Stage 2: Macro Equation Impact

Deconstruct which fundamental elements of Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity are affected, and verify that the accounting equation maintains mathematical equilibrium.

Stage 3: Normal Balance Translation

Map economic increases (+) and decreases (-) to the rules of Debit and Credit: Assets/Expenses/Drawings increase via Debit (Dr); Liabilities/Equity/Revenues increase via Credit (Cr).

Stage 4: General Journal Formulation

Formulate the formal chronological entry: Year, Month, Day; debited account title flush-left; credited account title indented 1/2 inch; Debit and Credit money amounts; concise objective explanation.

Stage 5: Dual Cross-Referenced Posting

Transfer amounts to the General Ledger accounts. Only when posting physically occurs is the Posting Reference (P/R) column filled with the account number, creating an unbreakable audit trail.

4.2.2 Anatomy of the Standard Two-Column General Journal

Below is a specimen page from the legal General Journal of Archer Stickers Hub (Page GJ-1). Observe how every line adheres to professional DLSU Accountancy standards:

4.2.3 The 5 Golden Execution Rules of Journalizing (Featuring the Blank P/R Rule)

  1. Debit Line First (Strictly Flush-Left): The title of every account to be debited is written strictly flush against the left margin of the "Account Titles and Explanation" column. The debit amount is placed on the exact same horizontal row in the Debit money column. If an entry has multiple debits, list all debits before any credit lines.
  2. Credit Line Indented: The account title to be credited is placed on the line immediately below the debits and indented approximately one-half inch (1.5 cm) to the right. This visual indentation immediately communicates to accountants and auditors that the account is credited, even before looking at the money columns.
  3. Concise, Objective Narration: A brief explanatory sentence follows every journal entry. Professional narrations cite the exact underlying commercial document (e.g., "per Sales Invoice #1045", "per Check Voucher #CV-101") so internal and external auditors can immediately locate physical supporting evidence.
  4. THE SACRED BLANK P/R RULE:
    Critical Internal Control Standard: The Posting Reference (P/R) column must remain COMPLETELY BLANK during Step 2 (Journalizing). It is filled in exclusively during Step 3 (Posting) when the number is physically copied into the ledger account. Entering the account number (e.g. 101) during journalizing falsely implies that the ledger has been updated, leading to catastrophic omissions when a bookkeeper is interrupted!
  5. Row Spacing Discipline: Leave exactly one blank line between distinct journal entries to visually compartmentalize separate business transactions. Never skip lines between debit and credit lines within the same transaction.

4.2.4 Simple vs. Compound Journal Entries (With Campus Case Studies)

Journal entries are categorized into two structural classes based on the number of accounts involved:

Simple Journal Entry

An entry involving exactly one debit and exactly one credit. Both amounts are identical.

Oct 7: Packaging Supplies Cash Purchase
Dr. Store Supplies ................. 3,000.00
    Cr. Cash in Bank ...................... 3,000.00
(To record cash purchase of sticker mailers)
Compound Journal Entry

An entry involving two or more debits, two or more credits, or both. Total debits must equal total credits (Total Dr = Total Cr).

Oct 21: Supplier Payment with 2% Cash Discount
Dr. Accounts Payable ............. 15,500.00
    Cr. Purchase Discounts ................. 310.00
    Cr. Cash in Bank .................... 15,190.00
(To record payment within discount window)
Another Classic Compound Case: Prompt Customer Settlement with 2% Sales Discount

On October 22, the DLSU USG settles the remaining ₱3,000.00 balance on their bulk sticker order within the 10-day discount window (2/10, n/30). They pay ₱2,940.00 in cash after deducting the ₱60.00 sales discount (2% of ₱3,000.00):

Oct 22   Cash in Bank ....................... 2,940.00
        Sales Discounts ..................... 60.00
            Accounts Receivable ................. 3,000.00
        (To record collection from DLSU USG within discount window)

4.2.5 The Asset Method vs. the Expense Method (When Payment Comes Before Use)

Many transactions have a payment point that comes before the purchase (use) point: the business pays first, and the benefit is consumed or sold later. This covers prepayments (prepaid rent, prepaid insurance), supplies, and inventories. For all of these, standard accounting practice permits two recognized recording methods, not just for merchandise:

The Asset Method (Balance Sheet approach)

At payment, debit an asset account (Prepaid Rent, Store Supplies, Merchandise Inventory). At period-end, an adjusting entry moves the portion already used or sold to expense.

The Expense Method (Income Statement approach)

At payment, debit an expense account (Rent Expense, Store Supplies Expense, Purchases). At period-end, an adjusting entry moves the portion still unused or unsold back to an asset.

📌 FDNACCT convention (used in all examples, exercises and the Solvers Lab)
  • Inventories: we use the Expense Method (debit 501 Purchases) so that the cost flows into the purchases accounts and, at period-end, into Cost of Goods Sold (the Periodic System).
  • Everything else (supplies and prepayments such as prepaid rent and prepaid insurance): we use the Asset Method (debit 103 Store Supplies, 104 Prepaid Rent, 106 Prepaid Insurance).
The other method remains valid, and you should recognize it, but unless a problem says otherwise, use these defaults.

Why the choice of method does not change the final result

First, a preview: what is an adjusting entry? (formally covered in Unit 4.7)

Every entry you have recorded so far was triggered by an actual event: cash was paid, goods were sold, a bill arrived. But some accounts become out of date simply because time passes or items get used up, even though no new transaction takes place. For example, you pay three months of rent on October 2. As October goes by, part of that rent is no longer a benefit you are waiting to receive; it has already been used. Nobody pays or receives anything on October 31, yet the books must show the correct amounts for the month.

The entry made at the end of the period to bring an account up to date is called an adjusting entry. Three things to remember for now:

  • It is made on the last day of the period (here, October 31), not when cash moves.
  • It never involves Cash. It only moves an amount between an asset account and an expense account.
  • Its job is to leave each account showing the correct amount: the asset shows only what is still unused, and the expense shows only what has been used up.

Example A: Prepaid rent

On October 2, Archer Stickers Hub pays ₱15,000 cash for 3 months of kiosk rent (October, November and December). By October 31, 1 month has been used (₱15,000 ÷ 3 = ₱5,000) and 2 months (₱10,000) are still unused. So the correct amounts at October 31 are: Prepaid Rent (asset) ₱10,000 and Rent Expense ₱5,000. Watch how each method reaches that answer:

StepAsset Method (debit an asset at payment)Expense Method (debit an expense at payment)

Cr. Cash 15,000

Rent Expense ₱15,000 → ₱10,000 too high

Cr. Rent Expense 10,000

Example B: Store supplies

On October 3, the business buys ₱4,500 of store supplies for cash. On October 31, a count shows supplies costing ₱1,500 are still on hand, so the amount used up is ₱4,500 − ₱1,500 = ₱3,000. The correct amounts at October 31 are Store Supplies (asset) ₱1,500 and Store Supplies Expense ₱3,000.

The takeaway
  • The two methods differ only in the first entry and, as a result, in the size and direction of the adjustment.
  • The Asset Method adjusts for the amount used up (asset → expense). The Expense Method adjusts for the amount still unused (expense → asset).
  • After the adjusting entry, the ending balances and therefore the financial statements are identical. That is why either method is acceptable; we simply standardize on the Asset Method for supplies and prepayments (see the FDNACCT convention above).
  • Inventories follow the same logic, with Purchases on one side and Merchandise Inventory on the other. That comparison, including the periodic and perpetual systems, is covered in detail in Unit 4.6.

4.2.6 The Liability Method vs. the Revenue Method (When Collection Comes Before Earning)

The mirror image of 4.2.5 occurs on the revenue side: when the collection point comes before the revenue point, the business is paid first and earns the revenue later. This is the case for unearned revenues (customer advances, deposits, prepaid subscriptions). Two recognized recording methods apply:

The Liability Method (Balance Sheet approach)

At collection, credit a liability (203 Unearned Revenue). As the goods or services are delivered, the earned portion is moved to revenue.

The Revenue Method (Income Statement approach)

At collection, credit a revenue account (401 Sales Revenue). At period-end, an adjusting entry moves the portion not yet earned back to a liability.

📌 FDNACCT convention

For unearned revenues, we generally use the Liability Method (credit 203 Unearned Revenue when the cash is collected). All examples, exercises and the Solvers Lab use it unless a problem says otherwise; the Revenue Method is shown so that you can recognize it.

Example: on October 11, Archer Stickers Hub receives ₱8,000 cash in advance for customized merchandise to be delivered next month. On October 23, goods worth ₱5,000 are delivered and the rest remains undelivered at October 31.

Point in time Liability Method (credit a liability) Revenue Method (credit a revenue)

Cr. 401 Sales Revenue 8,000

Cr. Unearned Revenue 3,000
(the ₱3,000 not yet earned)

Sales Revenue ₱5,000
Same outcome again

As with the asset and expense methods, the choice changes only the first entry. Once the period-end adjusting entries (Unit 4.7) are made, both methods report the same liability and the same revenue. In the Solvers Lab, Exercise 1 uses the FDNACCT defaults (Asset Method for prepayments and supplies, Liability Method for advances) but lets you switch to the alternative methods for practice.

4.2.7 The Commercial Source Document Spectrum & Internal Control Auditing

Every journal entry requires an authentic commercial document. Below is the evidentiary hierarchy used across the Archer Stickers Hub enterprise:

Official Receipt (OR)

Legal proof of cash collections or payments under BIR regulations. Issued by Archer Stickers Hub when customers pay cash; received by Archer Stickers Hub when paying rent or suppliers.

Commercial Sales Invoice (SI)

Billing document evidencing the transfer of ownership of goods. Accompanies credit sales to student organizations (e.g. DLSU USG, Rotaract) and credit purchases from Manila Vinyl Supply.

Promissory Note (PN)

A formal, unconditional written promise signed by the maker to pay a definite sum of money on demand or at a fixed future date, typically carrying explicit interest (e.g., equipment purchase, bank loan).

Credit Memorandum (CM)

Issued to inform a buyer that their account receivable has been credited (reduced) due to returned defective stickers or price allowances.

Debit Memorandum (DM)

Issued to inform a seller that their accounts payable has been debited (reduced) due to defective goods returned or special deductions.

Check Voucher (CV)

An internal authorization voucher detailing approved payee, invoice numbers, discounts, and net check disbursement amount prior to signing checks.

💡 Formative Drill 4.2: The Blank P/R Rule & Merchandising Method Micro Check

Why does internal audit protocol strictly forbid an accounting clerk from entering account numbers into the General Journal's P/R column while journalizing transactions, and how does the Expense Method classify initial stock purchases?

Correct! The P/R entry in the journal is an audit checkmark confirming that the amount was transferred to the ledger. Leaving it blank until posting ensures that interrupted clerks never accidentally omit postings! Furthermore, the periodic expense method records stock acquisitions as Purchases (affecting Equity) until physical count.
UNIT 4.3 STEP 3 OF ACCOUNTING CYCLE

Posting to the General Ledger & Ledger Systems Architecture

Executive Summary & Information Storage
Step 3 of the accounting cycle is Posting—the process of transferring journalized debit and credit figures from the General Journal to their specific individual accounts in the General Ledger (the Book of Final Entry). While the journal organizes transactions chronologically as a financial diary, the ledger organizes data by account classification (Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Revenues, Expenses). Today's commercial standard is the Running Balance Ledger Format (3-column or 4-column), which computes a cumulative ending balance after every single posting. Cross-referencing between journal pages and ledger account numbers establishes an unbreakable, dual-directional audit trail.

4.3.1 Chart of Accounts (COA) Block Numbering Architecture

Before any business transaction can be posted, an enterprise must establish its structural directory: the Chart of Accounts (COA). The Chart of Accounts is a systematically numbered listing of every account title recognized by the business, defining its assigned numerical identifier, account category, and normal balance. Enterprise accounting designs incorporate flexible block numbering with deliberate gaps between numbers to accommodate future expansion:

100–199: ASSETS (Normal Bal: Debit)
  • 101: Cash in Bank (BDO)
  • 102: Accounts Receivable
  • 103: Store Supplies
  • 104: Prepaid Rent
  • 105: Merchandise Inventory
  • 106: Prepaid Insurance
  • 107: Notes Receivable
  • 108: Interest Receivable
  • 150: Store Equipment
  • 151: Accum. Depreciation (Cr)
200–299: LIABILITIES (Normal Bal: Credit)
  • 201: Accounts Payable
  • 202: Notes Payable
  • 203: Unearned Revenue
  • 204: Interest Payable
  • 210: Salaries Payable
  • 220: Utilities Payable
300–399: OWNER'S EQUITY
  • 301: Dela Cruz, Capital (Cr)
  • 302: Dela Cruz, Drawings (Dr)
  • 350: Income Summary (Closing)
400–499: REVENUES (Normal Bal: Credit)
  • 401: Sales Revenue
  • 402: Sales Returns & Allowances (Dr)
  • 403: Sales Discounts (Dr)
  • 404: Interest Income (Cr)
500–699: COST OF SALES & EXPENSES (Normal Bal: Debit)
  • 500: Cost of Goods Sold (Perpetual)
  • 501: Purchases
  • 502: Freight-In
  • 503: Purchase Returns & Allowances (Cr)
  • 504: Purchase Discounts (Cr)
  • 601: Salaries Expense
  • 602: Rent Expense
  • 603: Utilities Expense
  • 604: Advertising Expense
  • 605: Taxes and Licenses Expense
  • 606: Store Supplies Expense
  • 607: Delivery Expense
  • 608: Interest Expense
  • 609: Insurance Expense
The Architectural Logic of Deliberate Gaps

Notice why account numbers jump (e.g., from 105 to 150, or 203 to 210). In professional systems design, gaps are intentionally reserved for future accounts. If Archer Stickers Hub later introduces Short-Term Marketable Securities (an asset), it can be assigned code 110 without disturbing the existing numbering of Store Equipment (150).

4.3.2 General Ledger: The Storehouse of Accounts by Classification

If management asks Chris Dela Cruz: "How much cash do we currently have in BDO?" or "What is our total outstanding trade debt to Manila Vinyl Supply?", scanning through hundreds of chronological journal entries would be absurdly inefficient. The General Ledger solves this by aggregating all historical changes for each specific asset, liability, equity, revenue, and expense into its own dedicated record:

General Journal (Book of Original Entry)
  • Organized chronologically by transaction date.
  • Shows the complete dual impact of each transaction in one place.
  • Contains full narrative descriptions and source document citations.
  • The P/R column references the Ledger Account Number (e.g. 101).
General Ledger (Book of Final Entry)
  • Organized by account topic in Chart of Accounts sequence.
  • Shows the cumulative balance and complete activity history for each account.
  • Narrations are condensed into brief item codes to optimize space.
  • The P/R column references the Journal Page Number (e.g. GJ-1).

4.3.3 T-Accounts vs. The Commercial Running Balance Ledger Format

In classroom scratchpads, accountants sketch informal T-Accounts. However, in formal corporate audits, BIR compliance, and modern ERP software (SAP, Oracle, NetSuite), the Running Balance Form is legally mandated. Below are two authentic specimen accounts from the General Ledger of Archer Stickers Hub:

4.3.4 The 4-Phase Posting Mechanics & Unbreakable Audit Trail

For every line item in the General Journal, execute the following 4 steps in exact chronological sequence:

  1. Locate Account & Record Date: Turn to the dedicated General Ledger account matching the journal line item. Enter the transaction date in the ledger's Date column.
  2. Post the Monetary Amount: Enter the exact peso figure into the Debit column (if debited in the journal) or Credit column (if credited in the journal).
  3. Compute Updated Running Balance:
    • If the account has a normal Debit balance (Assets, Expenses, Drawings): Add debits, subtract credits (New Balance = Prior Balance + Debit − Credit).
    • If the account has a normal Credit balance (Liabilities, Equity, Revenues): Add credits, subtract debits (New Balance = Prior Balance + Credit − Debit).
  4. Complete the Dual Cross-Reference (The Audit Lock):
    • In the Ledger's P/R column: Write the Journal Page (e.g. GJ-1). This tells the auditor where the transaction originated.
    • In the Journal's P/R column: Write the Ledger Account Number (e.g. 101). This confirms to the auditor that posting is complete.

4.3.5 Control Accounts vs. Subsidiary Ledgers (The "Ledger Within a Ledger")

If Archer Stickers Hub sells stickers on account to 50 student organizations and owes 20 different suppliers, displaying every individual customer and supplier in the main General Ledger would cause catastrophic information overload. Financial statements would become cluttered with dozens of micro-accounts.

Accounting architecture resolves this through a two-tiered hierarchy: a General Ledger Control Account (the macro summary) supported by a Subsidiary Ledger (the micro detail, or "a ledger within a ledger"):

General Ledger Control Account (Macro)

A single summary account in the General Ledger (e.g., Accounts Receivable - Acct #102). Its ending balance reflects the aggregate debt owed by all customers combined at any point in time.

GL Control Balance (Oct 31): ₱4,400.00 Dr
Subsidiary Ledger: Customer Cards (Micro)

A dedicated binder or digital database containing an individual running balance card for each specific customer (DLSU USG, DLSU Rotaract, Debate Society), tracking their specific invoices, partial payments, and price allowances.

Sum of Subledger Cards = ₱4,400.00 Dr (Exact Tie-Out)

UNIT 4.4 STEP 4 OF ACCOUNTING CYCLE

Preparing the Unadjusted Trial Balance & Mathematical Error Diagnostics

Executive Summary & Detective Protocols
Step 4 of the accounting cycle is preparing the Unadjusted Trial Balance. It is an internal financial working schedule listing all open General Ledger accounts and their ending balances in two columns (Debits and Credits) at a specific calendar date. Its primary operational purpose is to verify mathematical double-entry equality (Total Debits = Total Credits). While equality is mandatory, it is not sufficient—a balanced trial balance does not prove that all transactions were recorded, that authentic documents were used, or that PFRS principles were upheld. Accountants apply mathematical detective protocols—the Rule of 2 and the Rule of 9—to quickly isolate posting and transcription errors.

4.4.1 Architectural Role, Ending Balances & Chart of Accounts Alignment

The Unadjusted Trial Balance serves as the vital bridge connecting routine transaction recordkeeping (Steps 1–3) with period-end accrual reporting (Steps 5–8). Students must recognize two foundational principles:

  1. The Trial Balance is Structurally the Chart of Accounts: It is not a new or separate ledger. Rather, it is literally the enterprise's Chart of Accounts populated with the net ending debit or credit balance that accumulated in each active ledger account during the accounting period.
  2. Beginning Balance to Ending Balance Progression: Every account begins with an opening balance (for a new venture like Archer Stickers Hub established on October 1, 2026, all beginning balances are ₱0.00). Throughout the period, business operations add debits and credits. At period-end, each account is footed, and its net unadjusted ending balance is extracted to the Trial Balance:
    Ending Balance = Beginning Balance + Additions − Deductions

The schedule follows a formal Three-Line Heading:

  • Line 1: Name of the Enterprise (e.g., Archer Stickers Hub).
  • Line 2: Title of the Schedule (e.g., Unadjusted Trial Balance).
  • Line 3: Specific Calendar Date (e.g., October 31, 2026). Notice this is a point in time ("As of October 31, 2026"), never a period ("For the month ended").

4.4.2 Real (Permanent) vs. Nominal (Temporary) Accounts

Examining the 21 accounts on Archer Stickers Hub's Trial Balance reveals a profound accounting dichotomy: some accounts represent continuous, long-term economic existence, while others merely measure performance for the current monthly cycle.

Real (Permanent) Accounts
  • Account Types: Assets (100s), Liabilities (200s), and Owner's Equity Capital (301).
  • Financial Statement: Statement of Financial Position (Balance Sheet).
  • Cumulative Nature: They measure economic resources and claims at a specific point in time.
  • Period-End Treatment: THEY ARE NEVER CLOSED. The ending balance of Cash on October 31 (₱62,800.00) becomes the beginning balance of Cash on November 1. Their life is continuous across accounting periods.
Nominal (Temporary) Accounts
  • Account Types: Revenues (400s), Cost of Sales & Expenses (500s–600s), and Owner's Drawings (302).
  • Financial Statement: Income Statement (Revenues & Expenses) and Statement of Changes in Equity (Drawings).
  • Period-Specific Nature: They act as temporary scoreboards measuring the operational performance of only one specific accounting period.
  • Period-End Treatment: CLOSED TO ZERO. At the end of the period (Step 7), their balances are transferred into Dela Cruz, Capital via the Income Summary clearing account. They begin November with a fresh ₱0.00 balance.

STEPS 7–8 PREPARATION

4.4.3 The Trial Balance Shield: What Equality Proves vs. What It Hides

Errors That UNBALANCE the Trial Balance (Total Dr ≠ Total Cr)
  • Single-Sided Entry: Only the debit or only the credit leg was posted to the ledger.
  • Unequal Money Posting: Posting ₱15,000 on debit and ₱1,500 on credit.
  • Wrong Column Placement: Placing an ₱8,000 debit balance in the Credit column of the trial balance (Discrepancy = 2 × ₱8,000 = ₱16,000).
  • Wrong Side Ledger Posting: Posting a credit entry to the debit side of an account.
  • Ledger Footing Error: Addition/subtraction math error when computing an account's running balance.
  • Omission of an Account: Accidentally skipping an open ledger account when preparing the trial balance schedule.
  • Transposition on Schedule: Writing ₱54,000 as ₱45,000 in one column of the schedule.
Errors That LEAVE the Trial Balance IN BALANCE (Total Dr = Total Cr)
  • Error of Total Omission: An entire transaction was completely omitted from both the journal and ledger.
  • Duplicate Entry: An entire valid transaction was journalized and posted twice.
  • Error of Commission: An entry was posted to the wrong account of the correct category (e.g. debiting Store Supplies instead of Store Equipment).
  • Error of Principle: Violating foundational accounting principles (e.g. debiting an operating expense instead of capitalizing a fixed asset).
  • Compensating Errors: Two unrelated errors of equal magnitude in different accounts accidentally cancel out.
  • Complete Inversion of Entry: Debited what should have been credited and credited what should have been debited for equal amounts.

4.4.4 Mathematical Diagnostic Protocols: The Rule of 2 & The Rule of 9

When Total Debits and Total Credits on the Unadjusted Trial Balance fail to balance, forensic accountants do not randomly re-add figures. Instead, they immediately compute the Net Discrepancy (D) and apply two algebraic diagnostic tests:

Fundamental Forensic Formula
Discrepancy (D) = | Total Debits − Total Credits |
The numerical properties of D reveal the exact category of bookkeeping malfunction before examining a single physical voucher.
➗ The Rule of 2
REVERSED COLUMN / D = 2X
Mathematical Principle: When an account with an authentic debit balance X is mistakenly entered in the Credit column (or vice versa), Debits lose X while Credits gain X. The resulting discrepancy is double the amount:
D = 2X   ⇒   X = D / 2
📌 Archer Stickers Hub Example:
  • True Balance: Prepaid Rent (Acct 104) has debit balance X = ₱12,000.00.
  • Posting Blunder: Listed in the Credit column on the Trial Balance.
  • Trial Balance Result: Total Debits = ₱172,710.00; Total Credits = ₱196,710.00.
  • Discrepancy (D): |172,710 − 196,710| = ₱24,000.00.
  • Diagnostic Resolution:
    1. Check: D (₱24,000.00) is an even number.
    2. Compute: X = D / 2 = ₱24,000 / 2 = ₱12,000.00.
    3. Action: Search Trial Balance for an account with balance ₱12,000.00.
    4. Fix: Shift Prepaid Rent to Debit; difference becomes ₱0.00!
💡 Key Takeaway: An even discrepancy always calls for an immediate division by 2.
🔄 The Rule of 9
TRANSPOSITIONS & SLIDES / D / 9
Mathematical Principle: Any base-10 digit flip (transposition) or decimal displacement (slide) creates an error whose difference is evenly divisible by 9:
D / 9 = Integer   ⇒   Transposition or Slide
📌 Archer Stickers Hub Examples:
Case A: Transposition (Swapped Adjacent Digits)
• Store Supplies true balance: ₱7,500.00
• Entered erroneously as: ₱5,700.00 (7 and 5 swapped)
• Discrepancy: D = |7,500 − 5,700| = ₱1,800.00
• Quotient: 1,800 / 9 = 200 (Integer! Leading digits differ by 2: 7 − 5 = 2).
Case B: Transplacement / Slide (Moved Decimal Place)
• Salaries Expense true balance: X = ₱3,500.00
• Entered erroneously as: ₱35,000.00 (decimal moved 1 place right)
• Discrepancy: D = |35,000 − 3,500| = ₱31,500.00
• Quotient: 31,500 / 9 = ₱3,500.00 = X! (Quotient immediately reveals the exact base amount!).
💡 Key Takeaway: If D is divisible by 9, divide by 9. If the quotient matches an account balance, it is a slide; otherwise, it is a transposition!
QUICK FORENSIC DIAGNOSTIC MATRIX: UNBALANCED TRIAL BALANCE
Error Nature Mathematical Formula Diagnostic Test Auditor's Action Plan
Reversed Balance / Column Shift D = 2X Is D an even number? Divide D by 2. Scan ledger for account with balance equal to X.
Transposition Error (Digit Flip) D = 9(a − b) × 10k Is D / 9 an integer? Quotient indicates difference between swapped digits (e.g. 18/9 = 2 → digits differ by 2).
Slide Error (Decimal Shift) D = 9X or 0.9X Is D / 9 an account amount? Quotient D / 9 directly yields the true original transaction amount X.
Single-Sided Entry or Omission D = X Neither Rule of 2 nor 9 holds Scan journal for an entry with exact amount equal to D that was only posted once.

4.4.5 Correcting Journal Entries Protocol (3-Step Framework)

Bookkeeping errors inevitably occur in commercial operations. Under PFRS, accountants follow strict legal and professional protocols depending on the exact discovery milestone:

✏️ Discovered BEFORE Posting to Ledger

Draw a neat, single horizontal line through the incorrect word or figure, write the correct item immediately above, and place the bookkeeper's initials. Strict Audit Prohibition: Never erase, white-out, scribble over, or use correction fluid/tape on official accounting books!

📋 Discovered AFTER Posting to Ledger

Because the erroneous figures have already integrated into the General Ledger accounts, a formal Correcting Journal Entry must be entered into the General Journal with an explicit explanation and posted to the ledger to establish a permanent audit trail.

THE 3-STEP CORRECTING ENTRY ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORK
Systematic method to derive the exact correcting entry without distorting uncorrupted ledger accounts
AUDIT COMPLIANT
STEP 1: WHAT WAS RECORDED?

Write out the erroneous entry that was actually posted into the accounts to identify which specific accounts were improperly debited or credited.

STEP 2: WHAT SHOULD HAVE BEEN RECORDED?

Determine the correct PFRS journal entry that should have been made from the underlying commercial source document.

STEP 3: WHAT IS THE CORRECTING ENTRY?

Formulate the journal entry required to eliminate the erroneous balance and properly establish the correct account balance.

Campus Case 1: Display Equipment Mistakenly Recorded as Store Supplies (₱8,000.00 Cash)

On October 5, Archer Stickers Hub acquired heavy-duty aluminum display racks for ₱8,000.00 cash. An intern mistakenly journalized and posted the debit to Store Supplies (Acct 103) instead of Store Equipment (Acct 150). The cash payment was recorded correctly.

❌ Step 1: Erroneous Entry Actually in Books
Dr. Store Supplies (103) ........... 8,000.00
Cr. Cash (101) ............................... 8,000.00
Defect: Store Supplies overstated by ₱8k; Store Equipment omitted; Cash is correct!
✔️ Step 2: Correct PFRS Entry That Should Have Been Made
Dr. Store Equipment (150) .......... 8,000.00
Cr. Cash (101) ............................... 8,000.00
Objective: Put ₱8,000.00 into Equipment; remove ₱8,000.00 from Supplies; leave Cash alone.
✅ STEP 3: FORMAL GENERAL JOURNAL CORRECTING ENTRY (OCTOBER 31, 2026) POSTED TO GENERAL LEDGER
Date Account Titles and Explanation P/R Debit (₱) Credit (₱)
Oct 31 Store Equipment 150 8,000.00 —
Store Supplies 103 — 8,000.00
(To reclassify aluminum display racks purchased on Oct 5 previously misposted to store supplies. Cash account is accurate and unaffected.)
Campus Case 2: Credit Purchase Understated by ₱4,050.00 (Recorded ₱450 instead of ₱4,500)

On October 19, purchased ₱4,500.00 packaging supplies on 30-day credit from Quiapo Paper Supply (Tx #19). The entry was accidentally journalized and posted as ₱450.00 to both accounts (a slide/transplacement error leaving Trial Balance balanced, but both accounts understated by ₱4,050.00).

✅ STEP 3: FORMAL SUPPLEMENTAL CORRECTING ENTRY (OCTOBER 31, 2026) POSTED TO GENERAL LEDGER
Date Account Titles and Explanation P/R Debit (₱) Credit (₱)

💡 Formative Drill 4.4: Diagnostic Error Detection Micro Check

On the unadjusted trial balance of Archer Stickers Hub, Total Debits equal ₱195,510.00 and Total Credits equal ₱184,710.00 (Discrepancy = ₱10,800.00). Applying both the Rule of 2 and Rule of 9, what are the two most probable causes?

Correct! Discrepancy D = ₱10,800.00. By Rule of 2: 10,800 / 2 = ₱5,400.00, indicating a ₱5,400 credit balance was entered in the debit column. By Rule of 9: 10,800 / 9 = 1,200, indicating a transposition or slide error!
UNIT 4.5 PROMISSORY NOTES & NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS

Accounting for Promissory Notes — Notes Payable vs. Notes Receivable, The "Coupon" Concept, Legal Anatomy & Practical Mechanics

Executive Summary & Legal Framework
A Promissory Note is an unconditional written promise in writing made by one person (the Maker) to another (the Payee), signed by the maker, engaging to pay on demand, or at a fixed or determinable future time, a sum certain in money to order or to bearer (Philippine Negotiable Instruments Law, Act No. 2031, Sec. 184 & Civil Code Art. 1157). Unlike open-account trade debt, a promissory note is a formal commercial contract that typically bears a stated annual interest rate known in financial terminology as the "Coupon". Promissory notes split cleanly into two distinct, non-confusing accounting perspectives: the Maker (debtor/borrower who books a Note Payable liability) and the Payee (creditor/lender who books a Note Receivable asset).

4.5.1 The Evolution of Trade Debt: Open Accounts vs. Promissory Notes & The "Coupon"

Students often confuse Accounts Payable / Receivable with Notes Payable / Receivable. In professional commercial practice, they represent two fundamentally different levels of legal formality, credit security, and financing cost:

💳 Accounts Payable vs. Notes Payable (The Debtor's Books)

Accounts Payable (Acct 201) is a generic, open-ended trade liability. It is born informally when a business receives inventory, supplies, or utility services on credit, evidenced only by an ordinary commercial invoice and delivery receipt. During the standard credit window (e.g., 2/10, n/30), it carries zero interest.

When the debtor signs an explicit, legally binding written IOU promising payment on a specified future date, the generic liability formalizes into a Notes Payable (Acct 202). Because the creditor ties up working capital for an extended term, a promissory note typically carries an interest charge known in banking and capital markets as a "Coupon" (the stated annual percentage rate printed on the face of the note).

📑 Accounts Receivable vs. Notes Receivable (The Creditor's Books)

Accounts Receivable (Acct 102) represents open customer obligations arising from ordinary sales or services on account. It is uncollateralized, non-negotiable, and does not yield interest revenue. In court, proving open accounts requires assembling purchase orders, delivery receipts, and billing statements.

A Notes Receivable (Acct 107) is a formal negotiable instrument held as an asset. When a customer seeks an extension on an overdue invoice, the seller replaces the open claim with a signed promissory note. This elevates legal recoverability and entitles the seller to earn Interest Income (Acct 404) via the note's stated coupon rate, compensating the merchant for the time value of money.

COMMERCIAL COMPARISON MATRIX: OPEN TRADE DEBT VS. PROMISSORY NOTES
Dimension Accounts Payable / Receivable (Open Account) Notes Payable / Receivable (Promissory Note)
1. Underlying Instrument Informal commercial invoice, purchase order, and delivery receipt. Formal, signed, negotiable written promissory instrument (unconditional IOU).
2. Interest Feature ("Coupon") Generally non-interest bearing (zero coupon) during agreed credit terms. Typically interest-bearing with a stated annual percentage rate ("coupon").
3. Typical Tenor & Terms Very short term: 10, 30, or 60 days (e.g., 2/10, n/30). Specified duration: 30, 60, 90, 180, or 360 days, or multiple months.
4. Legal Standing in Court Requires proof of delivery, acceptance, and invoice reconciliation. Self-proving negotiable instrument; prima facie evidence of debt under NIL Act 2031.
5. Liquidity & Discounting Cannot be easily sold or discounted at commercial banks. Can be endorsed and discounted at commercial banks for immediate cash liquidity.

Every valid promissory note is an official commercial negotiable instrument governed by Section 184 of the Negotiable Instruments Law (Act No. 2031). 🔴 The Note Payable Perspective (The Maker / Debtor)
  • Party Role: The Maker (Archer Stickers Hub / Juan Dela Cruz) who signs the promise.

  • Financial Cost: Incurs Interest Expense (Acct 608) for borrowing capital.
  • Initial Recording: Debits Cash or Asset; Credits Notes Payable strictly at Face Value (₱30,000.00).
🔵 The Note Receivable Perspective (The Payee / Creditor)
  • Party Role: The Payee (DLSU Commercial Leasing Corp.) entitled to collect.
  • Account Created: Notes Receivable (Acct 107) — a formal Current Asset.
  • Financial Return: Earns Interest Income (Acct 404) as compensation for time.
  • Initial Recording: Debits Notes Receivable strictly at Face Value (₱30,000.00); Credits Cash or Revenue.

4.5.5 The Simple Interest Formula & Civil Code Article 13 Day Count

THE SIMPLE INTEREST FORMULA: I = P × R × T
I (Interest) Peso Cost / Return
=
P (Principal) Face Value of Note
×
R (Coupon Rate) Annual Stated Rate %
×
T (Time Fraction) Days/360 or Mos/12
Standard Commercial Denominators (Time Fraction T)
  • Ordinary / Banker's Rule (Default): Uses 360 days in the denominator (Days / 360). Standard commercial practice in Philippine accounting unless exact interest is explicitly stipulated.
  • Exact Interest: Uses 365 days (or 366 for leap years) in the denominator (Days / 365). Used primarily by government treasury bills and central banks.
  • Monthly Tenor: When tenor is stated in months (e.g., 4 months), use 12 as the denominator (Months / 12).
Maturity Date Countdown Algorithm (Civil Code Art. 13)

Legal Rule: Exclude the date of issuance; include the date of maturity. Example for a 90-day note issued on October 1, 2026:

  • Days remaining in October: 31 − 1 = 30 days.
  • Days in November: 30 days (Cumulative = 30 + 30 = 60 days).
  • Days required in December: 90 − 60 = 30 days.
  • Maturity Date: December 30, 2026.

💡 Formative Drill 4.5: Note Dishonor Valuation Micro Check

When a maker defaults on a ₱50,000, 10%, 90-day note (using 360 days ordinary interest), at what amount does the payee debit Accounts Receivable upon dishonor?

UNIT 4.6 MERCHANDISING OPERATIONS & INVENTORY SYSTEMS

Accounting for Merchandising Operations — Periodic vs. Perpetual Systems, Freight Pipeline & Modern CIF, Trade vs. Cash Discounts, Month-End Reclassification & Ledger Convergence

Executive Summary & Merchandising Framework
Unlike service firms that generate revenue solely by performing labor, merchandising enterprises derive income by purchasing finished physical goods from wholesalers and reselling them to customers at a profit markup. Merchandising accounting operates on two foundational pillars:
1. Inventory Accounting Systems: The Periodic System (which applies the Expense Method to purchases) vs. the Perpetual System (which applies the Asset Method to purchases); and
2. Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) Dynamics: The systematic flow of physical merchandise from Beginning Inventory + Net Purchases → Total Goods Available for Sale (TGAS) → split between unsold stock (Ending Inventory on the Balance Sheet) and sold stock (Cost of Goods Sold on the Income Statement).
3. The Convergence Law: Although Periodic and Perpetual take totally different operational paths during the month, they produce mathematically identical balances across all accounts (Cash, Receivables, Payables, Inventory, Sales, COGS, and Net Income) upon completing month-end closing!

4.6.1 The Fundamental Divide: Expense Method (Periodic) vs. Asset Method (Perpetual)

Students often ask: "Why are there two completely different ways to record merchandise purchases?" The answer connects directly to a crucial conceptual choice introduced in our earlier units: the Expense Method vs. Asset Method.

💡 Recalling the Unit 4.2 Practice Simulator (Archer Stickers Hub)

Recall that in our Unit 4.2 practice simulation (the Archer Stickers Hub simulator), the instructions explicitly required us to record merchandise inventory purchases using the Expense Method. When Chris Dela Cruz purchased batches of vinyl stickers from Manila Vinyl Supply Co. on account, we debited the temporary nominal expense account Purchases (Acct 501), rather than debiting the permanent balance sheet asset account Merchandise Inventory (Acct 105).

Meanwhile, for long-term items like store display racks or prepaid insurance, we applied the Asset Method (debiting Store Equipment 150 and Prepaid Insurance 106). In merchandising operations, this exact philosophical distinction defines whether an enterprise operates under the Periodic System or the Perpetual System!

📦 The Periodic Inventory System (The Expense Method)
  • Core Philosophy: Merchandise purchases are assumed to be immediately expensed costs of the current operating period.
  • Purchases Accounts: Purchases are debited to temporary nominal account Purchases (501). Inbound freight is booked in Freight-In (502). Defective returns credit Purchase Returns & Allowances (503). Prompt discounts credit Purchase Discounts (504).
  • Upon Making a Sale: Only ONE entry is recorded: Dr. Cash / Accounts Receivable, Cr. Sales Revenue at retail selling price. Inventory is never touched during daily sales transactions!
  • Inventory Balance in Ledger: The Merchandise Inventory (105) account remains completely frozen at its Beginning Inventory balance throughout the entire operating cycle.
  • Cost of Goods Sold: Cannot be looked up from any single ledger account! It must be calculated mathematically at period-end using the master COGS equation following a mandatory physical inventory count.
  • Ideal For: Bakeries, sari-sari stores, bookshops, and retail stalls with high-volume, low-unit-cost goods where continuous barcode scanning is impractical.
🔄 The Perpetual Inventory System (The Asset Method)
  • Core Philosophy: Merchandise purchases are immediately capitalized as an asset (inventory) on the Statement of Financial Position.
  • Merchandise Inventory Account: Debits Merchandise Inventory (105) directly upon acquisition. Freight-In is capitalized directly into inventory. Returns and discounts reduce inventory directly. Nominal purchase accounts (501, 502, 503, 504) do NOT exist!
  • Upon Making a Sale: TWO simultaneous entries are recorded for every single customer checkout:
    1. Dr. Cash / AR, Cr. Sales Revenue (at Retail Selling Price).
    2. Dr. Cost of Goods Sold (500), Cr. Merchandise Inventory (105) (at Cost).
  • Inventory Balance in Ledger: The Merchandise Inventory (105) account continuously and perpetually reflects the exact live cost of goods sitting on the shelves.
  • Cost of Goods Sold: Constantly updated in real time. The account Cost of Goods Sold (500) carries a running balance at all times.
  • Ideal For: Supermarkets, appliance centers, automobile dealerships, and modern POS-integrated retail chains utilizing optical barcode/RFID scanning.
ARCHITECTURAL COMPARISON: PERIODIC (EXPENSE METHOD) VS. PERPETUAL (ASSET METHOD)
Accounting Feature Periodic System (Expense Method) Perpetual System (Asset Method)
1. Initial Recording of Purchases Debits temporary nominal account: Purchases (501) Debits permanent real asset account: Merchandise Inventory (105)
2. Freight Paid on Inbound Stock Debits adjunct nominal account: Freight-In (502) Capitalized directly into asset: Merchandise Inventory (105)
3. Returns of Defective Stock Credits contra-cost account: Purchase Ret & Allow (503) Credited directly from asset: Merchandise Inventory (105)
4. Cash Discounts Taken Credits contra-cost account: Purchase Discounts (504) Credited directly from asset: Merchandise Inventory (105)
5. Entries at Date of Sale 1 Entry: Retail sales price (Cash/AR & Sales) 2 Entries: (a) Retail sales price, AND (b) Cost of Goods Sold & Inventory relief
6. Purpose of Physical Count Essential: Required mathematically to compute ending inventory and Cost of Goods Sold. Internal Control: Required to verify physical inventory against book records and detect inventory shrinkage/theft.
7. Period-End Closing Process Requires a multi-line compound closing entry (Transaction 6) to establish ending inventory, clear nominal purchases, and book COGS. No inventory adjusting entry needed; only nominal accounts (Sales, COGS, operating expenses) are closed to Income Summary.

4.6.2 Inbound Logistics & The Freight Matrix: FOB Terms, The Visual Pipeline & Modern CIF Context

Before examining the General Journal entries for merchandise purchases, we must first address transportation and freight accounting. Freight terms dictate who owns goods during transit and who legally pays the shipping carrier.

🚢 Visualizing the Supply Chain Pipeline & The Title Transfer Point
Logistics & Ownership Pipeline
🏭
1. Supplier / Factory
Laguna factory warehouse
⚓
2. Port of Origin
Supplier shipping dock
FOB SHIPPING PT
🚢 ✈️ 🚚
3. Transit / Carrier
Goods in transit on SLEX
🏢
4. Port of Destination
Manila central hub
🏬
5. Buyer / Storefront
Chris's campus stall
FOB DESTINATION
🚩 FOB Shipping Point (Title Passes at Point 2 — Origin)
  • Title Transfer: Title and risk pass to the buyer the moment carrier accepts goods at Point 2.
  • Ownership in Transit: BUYER legally owns goods during Step 3 (Transit).
  • Economic Cost: BUYER pays/absorbs shipping → debited to Freight-In (502) or capitalized into inventory.
  • Risk of Loss: If cargo is lost or damaged in transit, the buyer bears the loss and claims insurance.
🏁 FOB Destination (Title Passes at Point 5 — Delivery)
  • Title Transfer: Title and risk remain with seller until goods arrive and are accepted at Point 5.
  • Ownership in Transit: SELLER retains legal ownership during Step 3 (Transit).
  • Economic Cost: SELLER pays/absorbs shipping → debited to Freight-Out / Delivery Expense (607).
  • Risk of Loss: If cargo is lost or damaged in transit, the seller bears the loss and must replace goods.
🌐 Modern Commercial Context: Why "FOB" Feels Archaic & The Reality of CIF / Incoterms 2020:
If you haven't heard "FOB" in modern trade, that is completely natural! The term "Free On Board" (FOB) dates back centuries to maritime sailing laws when cargo was literally passed by rope over the ship's physical rail. In contemporary international business and global e-commerce, companies operate under modern Incoterms 2020 rules. In modern trade, you will almost exclusively encounter terms like:
• CIF (Cost, Insurance, and Freight): The seller arranges and pays for the cost of goods, maritime freight, AND marine insurance until the shipment reaches the buyer's port of destination. (Standard in containerized cargo).
• DDP (Delivered Duty Paid): The ubiquitous e-commerce door-to-door standard (e.g. Amazon, Shopee, Lazada) where the seller assumes 100% of transport costs, import duties, and transit risks until goods are handed to the buyer.
Why does introductory accounting still test FOB? Because introductory accounting textbooks and CPA licensure exams use FOB Shipping Point and FOB Destination as the classic legal benchmarks to teach the core principle: When does legal title pass, who carries goods on their balance sheet at year-end, and is freight capitalized (Freight-In) or expensed (Freight-Out)?
THE 4-QUADRANT FREIGHT GENERAL JOURNAL MATRIX (SHIPPING COST ₱2,500)
Freight Condition Legal Owner in Transit Cost Bearer BUYER'S Journal Entry SELLER'S Journal Entry
1. FOB Shipping Point, Collect Buyer Buyer Dr. Freight-In 2,500.00
    Cr. Cash in Bank 2,500.00 		(No Entry on Seller's Books)
2. FOB Shipping Point, Prepaid Buyer Buyer (Advanced by Seller) Dr. Freight-In 2,500.00
    Cr. Accounts Payable 2,500.00 		Dr. Accounts Receivable 2,500.00
    Cr. Cash in Bank 2,500.00
3. FOB Destination, Collect Seller Seller (Advanced by Buyer) Dr. Accounts Payable 2,500.00
    Cr. Cash in Bank 2,500.00 		Dr. Freight-Out 2,500.00
    Cr. Accounts Receivable 2,500.00
4. FOB Destination, Prepaid Seller Seller (No Entry on Buyer's Books) Dr. Freight-Out 2,500.00
    Cr. Cash in Bank 2,500.00

4.6.3 Trade Discounts vs. Cash Discounts: Accounting Rationale, Formulas & The Golden Rule

Merchandising transactions feature two distinct types of discounts that serve totally different commercial functions:

Trade Discounts (Unrecorded Catalog Price Adjustments)

Used by manufacturers and wholesalers to adjust published catalog prices for different classes of buyers (e.g. bulk wholesalers vs. small campus kiosks) without reprinting physical price books.

Accounting Rule: Trade discounts are NEVER recorded in any ledger account! Both buyer and seller record the transaction net of trade discounts at Invoice Price.

Chain Discount Formula: List ₱100,000 less 20% and 10%
Invoice Price = ₱100,000 × (1 − 0.20) × (1 − 0.10)
Invoice Price = ₱100,000 × 0.80 × 0.90 = ₱72,000.00
Single Equivalent Rate = 1 - 0.72 = 28% (Not 30%!)
Cash Discounts (Recorded Prompt Payment Incentives)

Incentives offered to encourage prompt cash settlement of accounts (e.g. credit terms 2/10, n/30: 2% cash discount if paid within 10 days; full balance due in 30 days).

Accounting Rule: Recorded upon payment. Buyer records Purchase Discounts (504) (Credit); Seller records Sales Discounts (403) (Debit).

⚠️ The Golden Freight Exclusion Rule:
Cash discounts apply strictly to the net price of merchandise! Freight charges and courier fees are NEVER subject to cash discounts. Always deduct returns and exclude freight before computing discount percentages!

Why is No Entry Needed Under Perpetual?
• Live Real-Time Asset Tracking: When the physical count was performed, the shelves held ₱23,032.00 of hoodies. In the Perpetual general ledger, Account #103 was already updated live after every purchase, freight, return, discount, and sale, and already stands at exactly ₱23,032.00!
• Live Expense Tracking: Cost of Goods Sold (Account #500) was already debited for ₱21,000.00 on October 18 at the moment of sale.
• Zero Shrinkage: Because physical inventory matches book inventory perfectly, no inventory shrinkage adjustment is necessary. The accounts are already 100% up to date!
(Physical count confirms book records; ledger is already current)

Students often harbor a natural misconception: "If Periodic debits Purchases while Perpetual debits Merchandise Inventory, won't the final company profits and balance sheets be different?"
The answer is an emphatic NO! The choice of inventory system is strictly an internal bookkeeping design choice. By the time month-end closing (Transaction 6) is completed, both systems arrive at the exact same peso balances across every single balance sheet and income statement account.

💎 The Golden Rule of Merchandising Systems: "Two Paths, One Destination"

Never let the mechanics confuse you:
• The Perpetual System is an Asset Method that updates inventory continuously with every single scan at checkout.
• The Periodic System is an Expense Method that ignores inventory during daily sales, accumulating purchases in temporary cost buckets until month-end.

Yet, in Transaction 6, when the physical count is taken and the reclassification entry is posted, every centavo converges! Ending Inventory is ₱23,032.00 on both balance sheets; Cost of Goods Sold is ₱21,000.00 on both income statements; and Gross Profit is ₱14,000.00 on both profit reports!

4.6.5 The Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) Schedule: The Relatable Cookie Story

Many students find the formal Schedule of Cost of Goods Sold intimidating because they see abstract numbers on a page. To make this intuitive, let us follow a simple, relatable real-world story: The Story of Archer Gourmet Cookies.

🍪 The Story of Archer Gourmet Cookies: Thinking in Quantities & Pesos
Standard Cost: ₱80.00 / Cookie

Chris Dela Cruz operates a gourmet cookie stall on the DLSU campus. Every artisanal chocolate-chip cookie costs exactly ₱80.00 to purchase from the central commissary bakery. Let us trace Chris's cookie inventory throughout October in terms of both physical quantity (cookies) and peso amounts (₱):

Step 1: The Leftovers (Beginning Inventory)
On Oct 1, Chris unlocks the stall with 100 cookies left over in the glass display jar from September:
100 cookies × ₱80 = ₱8,000.00.
Step 2: 3 Purchases During the Month
• Oct 5: Ordered 200 cookies @ ₱80 = ₱16,000 (+ ₱1,000 Grab delivery freight).
• Oct 12: Ordered 150 cookies @ ₱80 = ₱12,000.
• Oct 20: Ordered 250 cookies @ ₱80 = ₱20,000 (terms 2/10, n/30).
Total Gross Purchases: 600 cookies = ₱48,000.00.
Step 3: Defective Return & Cash Discount
• Oct 22: 20 crushed cookies from Purchase 3 returned to bakery: 20 × ₱80 = ₱1,600.00.
• Oct 28: Paid Purchase 3 early within discount window: 2% cash discount = ₱400.00.
Net Purchases: 580 cookies = ₱46,000.00.
Step 4: Total Goods Available for Sale (TGAS)
How many total cookies could Chris possibly have sold during October?
100 (beginning) + 580 (net purchases) = 680 cookies available!
In Pesos: ₱8,000 (beg) + ₱46,000 (net) + ₱1,000 (freight) = ₱55,000.00 TGAS.
Step 5: The Closing Physical Count & Cost of Goods Sold Reveal:
On October 31 at closing, Chris counts the cookies remaining in the stall. He finds 120 cookies unsold in the rack.
• What is the value of Ending Inventory on the Balance Sheet? 120 cookies × ₱80 = ₱9,600.00.
• If Chris had 680 cookies available to sell, and only 120 cookies remain unsold, how many cookies did customers eat?
680 Available − 120 Left = 560 COOKIES SOLD!
• What was the exact cost of those 560 cookies sold?
₱55,000 TGAS − ₱9,600 Ending Inventory = ₱45,400.00 COST OF GOODS SOLD!

    Less: Purchase Returns & Allowances (20 pcs) (1,600.00) Crushed cookies returned to vendor
    Less: Purchase Discounts — (400.00) Prompt settlement incentive (2%)
Net Purchases 580 pcs ₱ 46,000.00 Net delivered physical goods

Connecting the Cookie Story to General Journal Entries

Under the Periodic System, at month-end, the accountant prepares a compound closing entry to remove beginning inventory (₱8,000) and temporary purchase accounts, establish ending inventory (₱9,600) on the balance sheet, and transfer the net difference to Cost of Goods Sold (₱45,400):

Dr. Merchandise Inventory (Ending) ... 9,600.00
Dr. Purchase Returns & Allowances ... 1,600.00
Dr. Purchase Discounts ................. 400.00
Dr. Cost of Goods Sold ............... 45,400.00
    Cr. Merchandise Inventory (Beginning) ... 8,000.00
    Cr. Purchases ............................ 48,000.00
    Cr. Freight-In ........................... 1,000.00
Scope Notice: Cost Flow Assumptions (FIFO vs. Weighted Average)

In our foundational cookie illustration, all batches had a standard unit cost of ₱80.00. When purchase prices fluctuate over time (e.g. cookies purchased at ₱75, ₱80, and ₱85), accounting uses Cost Flow Assumptions such as FIFO (First-In, First-Out) or Weighted Average Cost.

Quiz 2 Scope Note: Detailed mathematical cost-flow tracking under FIFO and Weighted Average is an advanced inventory valuation topic covered exclusively in Quiz 3 / Financial Accounting 2. In Quiz 2, questions test your mastery of merchandising transactions, freight terms, discount calculations, and the structural COGS equation. Hence, we purposefully avoid complicating our core mechanics with cost flow layers here!

💡 Formative Drill 4.6: Freight-Out Classification Micro Check 1

Where is Freight-Out (Delivery Expense) classified on the Statement of Profit or Loss?

Correct! Freight-Out is an operating selling expense. Only Freight-In is added to purchases within Cost of Goods Sold; Freight-Out is strictly a delivery expense below Gross Profit.
💡 Formative Drill 4.6: Calculating Net Cost of Purchases Micro Check 2

A store reports: Gross Purchases ₱150,000; Purchase Returns ₱10,000; Purchase Discounts ₱3,000; Freight-In ₱8,000; Freight-Out ₱5,000. What is the Net Cost of Purchases?

Correct! Net Purchases = ₱150,000 − ₱10,000 − ₱3,000 = ₱137,000. Add Freight-In (₱8,000) = ₱145,000. Freight-Out (₱5,000) is a selling expense and must NEVER enter Cost of Goods Sold!

Quiz 2 Formula Quick-Reference Card

Promissory Notes Formulas
  • Interest: I = P × R × T
  • Ordinary Interest: T = Days / 360
  • Exact Interest: T = Days / 365
  • Monthly Terms: T = Months / 12
  • Maturity Value: MV = P + I
Merchandising Operations Formulas
  • Net Sales = Gross Sales - Sales Returns - Sales Discounts
  • Net Purchases = Purchases - Purchase Returns - Purchase Discounts
  • Net Cost of Purchases = Net Purchases + Freight In
  • TGAS = Beginning Inventory + Net Cost of Purchases
  • COGS = TGAS - Ending Inventory
  • Gross Profit = Net Sales - Cost of Goods Sold
